solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Suggests naughty kid is dishonest

blocks.note: an imp is a mischievous child
someone who is dishonest tells untruths

explanation.surface: Someone hints that a badly behaved child is being untruthful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suggests' reads as the verb of the sentence, but it is the definition; the rest splits into two pieces read in order.
explanation.definitionFit: To imply something is to hint at it indirectly, so the two verbs are straightforward synonyms in the third person.

clue.text: European abandoning loud hostelry

indicators.note: to abandon something is to leave it behind, so a letter departs from the word

blocks.note: a Finn is a native of Finland
f (forte) is the musical marking for loud

explanation.surface: A traveller from Europe leaves a noisy pub.
explanation.walkthrough: FINN with its F, the musical symbol for loud, taken away leaves INN.
explanation.definitionFit: A hostelry is an old-fashioned word for a pub or lodging house serving travellers, which an inn is.

clue.text: After ceremony, regularly revisit ancient city

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so every other letter is kept
one thing coming after another places it later in the sequence of letters

blocks.note: pomp is ceremonial splendour
the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Following some formal event, a tourist goes back to see an ancient ruined city.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of 'revisit' follow the ceremonial word, as 'After' instructs.
explanation.definitionFit: Pompeii was the Roman city near Naples buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79.

clue.text: Daughter getting into rocky isle does very little

indicators.note: rocky means unsteady or shaky, so the letters are shaken into a new order
getting into a place means entering it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: D is the standard abbreviation for daughter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A daughter arrives on a craggy island and lazes about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocky isle' looks like a description of scenery, but 'rocky' rearranges the letters of 'isle' to ILES, and D goes in after the I.
explanation.definitionFit: To idle is to laze about without working, so the verb matches a person who does very little.

clue.text: Combatant flogged? That is right

blocks.note: in British slang, to flog something is to sell it
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for 'that is'
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a fighter was whipped, and is told that is correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flogged' suggests whipping, but in everyday British slang flogging something means selling it.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier is a member of an army who fights in battle, a straightforward example of a combatant.

clue.text: A-lister making a comeback? Botheration!

indicators.note: a comeback runs back the way it came, so the letters go in the opposite direction

blocks.note: an A-lister is a top celebrity

explanation.surface: A faded celebrity attempts a return to fame, and someone groans in annoyance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making a comeback' sounds like a career revival; here it turns the word backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of annoyance or frustration used when something goes wrong.

clue.text: To an extent, Harris hindered election loser

indicators.note: only to an extent means partly, so just part of the run of letters is used

blocks.note: the end of the first word plus the start of the second

explanation.surface: A comment that the Democratic candidate Harris was partly held back in her election campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: Kamala Harris lost the 2024 US election, a tempting misdirection; the answer is Rishi Sunak, whose Conservatives lost the 2024 UK general election.
explanation.definitionFit: Rishi Sunak, as British prime minister, led his party to defeat in the 2024 general election.

clue.text: Object about reckless and humiliating defeat

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: a thing is an object
rash means acting without care

explanation.surface: Someone protests about a careless, embarrassing loss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object' looks like a verb meaning protest, but it is a noun here, and 'about' tells it to wrap round the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrashing in sport is a heavy, one-sided loss, so it is a synonym for a crushing, humiliating defeat.

clue.text: Walls of eastern auditorium enthral, displaying glossy material

indicators.note: walls stand at the edges of a space, so only the outside letters of each word are kept

blocks.note: first and last letters
first and last letters
first and last letters

explanation.surface: The decorated walls of an eastern concert hall captivate visitors with their shine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walls of' applies to all three following words, taking the outer pair of letters from each in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Enamel is a hard, shiny coating fused onto metal or pottery, or a gloss paint, so it is a glossy substance.

clue.text: Girl hosting old monarch beams

indicators.note: a host takes guests in, so one piece holds another inside it

blocks.note: a lass is a girl, chiefly in northern English and Scottish use
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the royal cipher of the late Queen

explanation.surface: A young woman entertaining an elderly king smiles broadly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beams' looks like a verb for smiling, but it is the plural noun for shafts of light.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasers produce narrow, intense shafts of light, so they are examples of beams in the plural noun sense.

clue.text: Strong drinks on the house for mavericks

blocks.note: something on the house is given without charge
spirits are distilled alcoholic drinks

explanation.surface: A bar hands out complimentary hard liquor to its unconventional regulars.
explanation.walkthrough: The two pieces are read in reverse clue order: liquor given away gratis.
explanation.definitionFit: Mavericks and free spirits are both independent people who refuse to follow conventions or rules.

clue.text: Boxer possibly boxing on ship

indicators.note: to box something is to pack it in a case, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a boxer is one kind of fighter, hence 'possibly'
re means on or concerning, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: A prizefighter perhaps spars in a match aboard a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxing' seems to continue the boxer idea, but it means enclosing. RE, meaning 'about' or 'on', is a common crossword stand-in.
explanation.definitionFit: A freighter is a cargo vessel built to carry goods, so it is a type of ship.

clue.text: Dancing around, aren’t I a bit of a looker?

indicators.note: dancing around means moving about freely, so the letters swap places

blocks.note: the letters taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone twirling on the dance floor asks whether they are rather attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of a looker' sounds like 'quite attractive', but read literally it is a part of the eye, the organ one looks with.
explanation.definitionFit: The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, literally one part of the organ used for looking.

clue.text: Complaint made by topless Americans who deliver letters on time

indicators.note: topless means without a top, and in a down answer the top is the first letter, so it goes

blocks.note: mailman is the American word for postman
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A grievance is raised by American postal workers going shirtless while still being punctual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' suggests a grievance, but it is meant in the medical sense of an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint in the medical sense is an illness or disorder, which is exactly what an ailment is.

clue.text: Losing grand, cultivating dry fruit

indicators.note: to lose something is to no longer have it, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: G is slang shorthand for a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars
to raise crops is to cultivate them

explanation.surface: A grower loses a thousand pounds while farming dried fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: RAISING without its G leaves the answer; 'grand' is a thousand, abbreviated G.
explanation.definitionFit: A raisin is a dried grape, so it is one example of dried fruit.

clue.text: Parrot or ape? It inhabits India and China

indicators.note: something that inhabits a place lives within it, so it sits inside another piece

blocks.note: I is India in the NATO phonetic alphabet
in cockney rhyming slang, china plate means mate, a friend
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about which animal, parrot or ape, lives in India and China.
explanation.walkthrough: The animals and countries are all misdirection: 'Parrot or ape' are both verbs, and 'china' for friend is cockney rhyming slang (china plate rhymes with mate).
explanation.definitionFit: To parrot or to ape someone is to copy their words or behaviour, so both verbs mean to copy.

clue.text: Appealing ladies perhaps hugged by Wenceslas?

indicators.note: something hugged is held in someone's arms, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: the carol calls him Good King Wenceslas
the ladies is a women's toilet, an example of a loo

explanation.surface: Attractive women are perhaps embraced by the saintly Bohemian duke.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English 'the ladies' is a women's public toilet and a loo is any toilet; 'perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Appealing in the sense of attractive to look at, describing someone handsome or pretty, matches the adjective exactly.

clue.text: Travel around York’s middle part

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its centre, so only the inner letters are kept

blocks.note: the two central letters of the four
a bit is a part of something

explanation.surface: A visitor tours the central part of the city of York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Travel around' reads as sightseeing, but it is the definition, as a planet goes round the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: To orbit is to move in a circular path round something, as satellites circle planets.

clue.text: Ex-president with First from Oxford and two degrees

indicators.note: the first from a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: initial letter
BA (Bachelor of Arts) and MA (Master of Arts)

explanation.surface: A former head of state boasts a first-class Oxford degree and two more besides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' looks like a first-class degree, which fits the surface, but it only takes the opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Barack Obama served as US president from 2009 to 2017, so he is a former holder of that office.

clue.text: Firm where a lad works

blocks.note: first meaning: steady, secure, not wobbling
second meaning: a young groom who looks after racehorses in their building

explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a company employing a boy, but it is the adjective; a stable lad is the British term for a racehorse groom.
explanation.definitionFit: Firm means steady and secure as an adjective, and the horses' building is where a stable lad is employed.

clue.text: Conflict interrupting publicity for the Oscars, say

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: ads, advertisements, are publicity
a war is an armed conflict

explanation.surface: A quarrel disrupts the promotional campaign for the Academy film ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks the Oscars as one example of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oscars are the Academy Awards, given annually for achievement in film, so they are an example of prizes.

clue.text: Boring intro from Doors track

indicators.note: an intro is the opening of a song, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: initial letter
RY is an abbreviation for railway, a kind of track

explanation.surface: A listener finds the opening of a song by the rock band the Doors dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Track' suggests a song, but it means a railway line, abbreviated RY.
explanation.definitionFit: A dry speech or book is dull and uninteresting, so the adjective is a synonym for tedious.

clue.text: Cruel person for the most part is not sweet

indicators.note: the most part of something is nearly all of it, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a brute is a savagely cruel person

explanation.surface: A remark that a cruel person is mostly lacking in sweetness of nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not sweet' sounds like a comment on character, but it is a wine term.
explanation.definitionFit: Brut is the label for very dry champagne or sparkling wine, meaning it has little residual sugar.

clue.text: Essay covering old kind of literary work

indicators.note: a cover goes over and around something, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: an essay can mean an attempt, a try
aged means old

explanation.surface: A student's essay discusses an old genre of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essay' looks like a school composition, but it is used in its older sense of an attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Tragedy is a genre of drama or fiction ending in disaster for the protagonist, so it is one type of literature.
